title: An encyclopedia of human enhancer-gene regulatory interactions

items.q: What resource does this paper present?
items.a: A resource of more than 92 million enhancer-gene (E-G) regulatory interactions across 1,458 biosamples covering 369 cell types and tissues. It was built by integrating predictive models, chromatin states, 3D contacts and large-scale genetic perturbations generated by the ENCODE Consortium.
items.info: The resource also includes benchmarking software, predictive models (ENCODE-rE2G) and insights into enhancer function.
items.concl: Iterative perturbations combined with supervised machine learning can build increasingly accurate predictive models of enhancer regulation.

items.q: Which ground-truth datasets did they assemble for benchmarking?
items.a: 10,356 element-gene pairs measured in CRISPR perturbation experiments, more than 30,000 fine-mapped eQTLs, and 569 fine-mapped GWAS variants linked to a probable causal gene.
items.info: Interpreting the model showed that, beyond enhancer activity and 3D enhancer-promoter contact, promoter class and enhancer-enhancer synergy also guide enhancer-promoter communication.

items.q: What gap does the paper address?
items.a: It is still hard to identify accurately which elements act as enhancers in a given cell type and which genes they regulate. Many earlier predictions lack information on their accuracy, have not been compared on common benchmarks, or have known accuracy limitations.
items.info: Enhancers probably contain most causal variants for common complex diseases, so linking them to genes matters for human genetics.
items.concl: The field needs larger genetic perturbation datasets and a community framework to evaluate, compare and improve models.

items.q: Which features did earlier models find important for predicting enhancer-gene interactions?
items.a: The strength of activating chromatin marks at an element ('enhancer activity') and how often the element physically contacts a nearby promoter ('3D contact').
items.info: It was still unclear which experimental assays estimate these features best, how important they are compared with other features, and what they reveal about mechanism.

items.q: Why are some existing predictive models hard to apply to new cell types?
items.a: Some need many cell types to be analysed at the same time, and others need a large number of experimental inputs in each cell type.
items.info: As a result, there was no E-G resource covering the hundreds of cell types and tissues profiled by ENCODE.

items.q: What is the difference between 'regulatory interactions' and 'physical interactions' in this paper?
items.a: Regulatory interactions come from genetic perturbations, where changing the element changes the gene's expression. Physical interactions are measured by contact assays such as Hi-C or ChIA-PET. The authors use only regulatory interactions as gold standards.
items.info: The authors note this as an important difference from some earlier benchmarking efforts.

items.q: What are the three components of the ENCODE E-G resource?
items.a: (1) ENCODE-rE2G, new supervised classifiers trained directly on CRISPR perturbation data. (2) A benchmarking framework built from CRISPR, eQTL and GWAS data. (3) Genome-wide E-G maps across 1,458 ENCODE DNase-seq biosamples.
items.info: At minimum, ENCODE-rE2G needs cell-type-specific DNase-seq plus a reference ENCODE Hi-C map averaged across many tissues.

items.q: How big is the atlas per biosample?
items.a: In total there are 92,176,227 interactions between distal elements and target genes. On average each biosample has 40,210 unique regulatory elements and 63,221 E-G interactions, which annotate 0.89% of the roughly 3 billion bp genome.
items.info: You can look up a gene to find its predicted enhancers, look up an element to find its predicted target genes, or find predicted cell types and target genes for noncoding variants.

items.q: How does the ENCODE-rE2G approach differ from earlier models?
items.a: Earlier models mostly used unsupervised enhancer-promoter correlations, molecular rules, or supervised learning on proxies such as 3D loops or gene expression. ENCODE-rE2G is a supervised classifier trained directly on CRISPR data in one cell type and then applied genome-wide and to new cell types.
items.info: The authors had used a similar approach before, but with a much smaller CRISPR dataset.

items.q: Which features go into the DNase-only ENCODE-rE2G model?
items.a: The features fall into six groups: chromatin state (DNase-seq at element and promoter), 3D contact frequency averaged across 65 ENCODE Hi-C datasets, the ABC score, genomic position (e.g. distance to the promoter), promoter class (ubiquitously expressed housekeeping gene or not), and nearby enhancers (e.g. activity of other elements within 5 kb).
items.info: Best-subset feature analysis kept 8 of the 12 candidate features. This regularizes the model while keeping its probability estimates calibrated.

items.q: What is ENCODE-rE2G Extended?
items.a: A version that uses 45 features for Tier 1 ENCODE cell types. These come from DNase-seq, histone ChIP-seq, cell-type-specific Hi-C and ChIA-PET, plus features from other models such as EpiMap and GraphReg.
items.info: The 45 features are available in K562 and GM12878.

items.q: What was the training dataset and how were positives and negatives defined?
items.a: 10,356 element-gene pairs tested with CRISPR in K562 cells. 471 were positives (462 CRISPRi, 9 CRISPR deletions) with a significant drop in expression of 1 to 93%. 9,885 were negatives with no significant drop even though the experiment had good power to detect effects above 15 to 25%.
items.info: Data from earlier studies were re-analysed and harmonized, and statistical power was computed for every tested pair. Models were trained with hold-one-chromosome-out cross-validation.

items.q: How were continuous scores turned into binary predictions?
items.a: They chose the score threshold that gives 70% recall on the CRISPR training data, as in earlier studies. At this threshold ENCODE-rE2G predicts an average of 63,221 E-G interactions and 40,210 enhancers per biosample (108,535 interactions and 38,923 enhancers for Extended).
items.info: Each score is the logistic regression's probability of a regulatory effect. Predictions include well-studied enhancers at the HBE1, GATA1 and MYC loci.

items.q: Which models were compared in the benchmark?
items.a: ENCODE-rE2G and 616 other models. These included ABC run with different ENCODE assays, published machine-learning models (EpiMap, GraphReg, CIA, Enformer, EPIraction), and simple baselines such as nearest expressed TSS or gene, 3D contact, or correlation of element and promoter accessibility across cell types.
items.info: There were three complementary benchmark datasets: CRISPR-validated pairs, fine-mapped eQTLs and fine-mapped GWAS variants.

items.q: How did ENCODE-rE2G perform on the K562 CRISPR data?
items.a: ENCODE-rE2G beat DNase-only ABC with averaged Hi-C: AUPRC 0.66 vs 0.56, and precision at 70% recall 58% vs 48% (P bootstrap = 0.0001). ENCODE-rE2G Extended beat ABC using DNase x H3K27ac with cell-type-specific Hi-C: AUPRC 0.74 vs 0.61, and precision 73% vs 56%.
items.info: Scores also correlated with measured CRISPR effect sizes (Pearson R -0.45 vs -0.40 for the DNase-only models). For the Extended model the text gives 'R = 0.48 versus -0.42'. The missing minus sign looks like a typo, which is unclear in the paper.
items.concl: ENCODE-rE2G and ENCODE-rE2G Extended reach state-of-the-art performance.

items.q: Which kinds of E-G pairs do all models, including ENCODE-rE2G, predict poorly?
items.a: Four kinds: (1) probable indirect effects (P direct < 0.9), which tend to be farther from the TSS; (2) small CRISPR effect sizes, meaning weak enhancers; (3) elements without H3K27ac, meaning non-canonical enhancers; (4) ubiquitously expressed genes, which respond less to enhancers.
items.info: The positive rate was 1.5% for ubiquitously expressed genes vs 7.6% for other genes. All models missed three well-characterized distal MYC enhancers almost 2 Mb from the TSS.

items.q: Does ENCODE-rE2G generalize beyond the K562 training data?
items.a: Yes. On held-out CRISPRi data from K562, WTC11, HCT116, GM12878 and Jurkat (4,405 pairs, 190 positives) it had significantly higher AUPRC (P bootstrap = 0.0003) and precision (P bootstrap = 0.0001) than DNase-only ABC. Its precision stayed similar to training (53.2% vs 54.8%).
items.info: Pairs shared with the training data were removed and differences in experimental design were adjusted for. Performance was weighted by each pair's probability of being a direct effect. The Fig. 2d legend gives 4,378 total pairs while the text says 4,405; the discrepancy is not explained.

items.q: How did the models do on fine-mapped eQTLs?
items.a: In GM12878 compared with GTEx lymphoblastoid eQTLs (n = 273), ENCODE-rE2G Extended and ENCODE-rE2G reached 31-fold and 25-fold enrichment at 15% recall, comparable with other good models. Across 11 more GTEx tissues, ENCODE-rE2G had mean enrichment 6.5 (range 3.5 to 11.4) and a higher mean recall of 16% (5 to 24%).
items.info: Recall is the fraction of eQTL variants that overlap an enhancer linked to the correct eGene. The text gives n = 273 and the Fig. 2e legend gives n = 239 (and n = 243 for recall); the reason is unclear.

items.q: How did ENCODE-rE2G do on GWAS variants?
items.a: Using 29,245 fine-mapped distal noncoding variants for 94 UK Biobank traits, K562 and GM12878 enhancers were 10.6-fold enriched for erythroid or immune trait variants, vs 9.6-fold for DNase-only ABC (P = 0.0001). For noncoding credible sets in 11 blood traits across 473 blood biosamples, it had the highest precision at finding target genes (68% vs 67%) and better recall (51% vs 41%).
items.info: The causal gene was defined by an independent coding variant associated with the same trait. GWAS genes tend to have larger phenotypic impact and lie farther away than eQTL genes.
items.concl: ENCODE-rE2G performs well on all three benchmark types, each of which has different strengths and limitations.

items.section: Results - Genome-wide maps of enhancer regulation
items.q: How far are predicted enhancers from their target genes?
items.a: Most predicted interactions are short-range: 24.1% are under 10 kb and 74.6% are under 100 kb. This matches the distance distributions of the CRISPR, eQTL and GWAS data.
items.info: Extended Data Fig. 6a gives a median of 37.091 kb and a mean of 85.143 kb across all 92,176,227 pairs.

items.section: Results - Genome-wide maps of enhancer regulation
items.q: Do 1D chromatin state annotations capture ENCODE-rE2G enhancers?
items.a: Often not. 18.5% of ENCODE-rE2G enhancers have DNase signal below the global median, probably because weak elements can still act when close enough to a promoter. As a result, chromHMM misses 40% and the cCRE Catalogue misses 66% of ENCODE-rE2G enhancers.
items.info: The same annotations miss 30% (chromHMM) or 12% (cCRE) of validated enhancer-gene pairs from the 2021 Nasser CRISPR dataset.

items.section: Results - Genome-wide maps of enhancer regulation
items.q: How many enhancers does a gene have, and how many genes does an enhancer regulate?
items.a: On average each gene has 5.91 predicted enhancers (median 3), and each enhancer regulates 1.57 genes (median 1).
items.info: Many interactions are highly cell-type-specific, more so than promoter or enhancer activity alone. Many enhancers also regulate different genes in different biosamples.

items.section: Results - Genome-wide maps of enhancer regulation
items.q: Do genes with many vs few enhancers differ in function?
items.a: Yes. Among genes expressed in 50% of biosamples, genes with at least five enhancers per cell type were enriched for cell-type-specific processes such as angiogenesis and neurogenesis. Genes with 1.5 or fewer were enriched for housekeeping processes such as rRNA processing and mRNA splicing.
items.info: Extremes: SHOX has 77.57 enhancers per biosample and DNAJC16 has 0.005.

items.section: Results - Linking variants to genes and cell types
items.q: Why are enhancer maps alone not enough to link GWAS variants to genes?
items.a: GWAS variants often overlap enhancers predicted to regulate several genes (average 2.9, maximum 34), and 59.8% of them regulate different genes in different cell types.
items.info: So they combined variant-to-gene links from ENCODE-rE2G with gene-function information from the polygenic priority score (PoPS).

items.section: Results - Linking variants to genes and cell types
items.q: How well does ENCODE-rE2G intersected with PoPS work?
items.a: Intersecting the top two ENCODE-rE2G genes with the top two PoPS genes predicted a target gene for 2,173 of 13,012 noncoding credible sets (PIP > 0.1). This covered 8,234 of 48,305 fine-mapped variants, a 3.71-fold enrichment over control variants. Precision for known links was 79%, which is 1.4-fold higher than ENCODE-rE2G alone and 2.3-fold higher than PoPS alone.
items.info: The combination had higher precision and comparable recall to the ABC-Max atlas, with new predictions for 1,044 credible sets. ENCODE-rE2G alone beat OpenTargets L2G on both precision and recall. PoPS predicts MAGMA gene scores from 57,543 gene-level features.

items.section: Results - Linking variants to genes and cell types
items.q: Give an example of ENCODE-rE2G predicting both the target gene and the causal cell type.
items.a: Variants for mean corpuscular haemoglobin (MCH) were 16.3-fold enriched in enhancers of haematopoietic multipotent progenitors. The MCH variant rs875741 (PIP = 0.50) was linked to CPEB4 in haematopoietic progenitors only, and not in B cells, T cells or K562.
items.info: CPEB4 is broadly expressed, but the variant falls in a progenitor-specific enhancer, which points to a blood-specific mechanism. The text says 'MHC-linked variant' at one point, apparently a typo for MCH. Other examples (TFRC, KIT, BCL11A) are in Supplementary Note 5.

items.q: Which features were most informative in ENCODE-rE2G?
items.a: The most informative feature groups were 3D contact and distance, and enhancer activity. The single most informative feature was the ABC score itself. Promoter class and enhancer-enhancer features also contributed.
items.info: Analyses included best-subset selection, leave-one-feature-out and sequential feature selection. The promoter-class result fits recent work showing promoter classes differ in sensitivity to distal enhancers.

items.q: Which assay best measures enhancer activity in the ABC model?
items.a: Out of 523 ENCODE 1D chromatin experiments in K562, DNase-seq performed best. ChIP-seq for the cofactors EP300, NCOA1 and NCOR1 and several TFs performed similarly. H3K27ac was the best histone ChIP-seq.
items.info: Each assay replaced DNase-seq in the activity term, with K562 ENCODE Hi-C used for contact in all models.

items.q: Which 3D contact estimate worked best?
items.a: Cell-type-specific ENCODE Hi-C (23 billion reads, 5-kb resolution) gave 53.3% precision at 70% recall. This beat the cross-cell-type average Hi-C (104 billion reads, 48%) and an inverse function of distance (44.3%).
items.info: Six contact methods were compared, including CTCF and Pol II ChIA-PET. Cell-type-specific Hi-C helped most for pairs more than 100 kb apart.

items.q: Is DNase-seq or ATAC-seq better as input, and what do extra assays add?
items.a: Models using DNase-seq beat models using ATAC-seq. Adding cell-type-specific H3K27ac and/or Hi-C improved performance, with a larger gain for ATAC-based models, suggesting DNase-seq is a better proxy for enhancer activity.
items.info: Adding Hi-C recovered 20 interactions the DNase-only model missed. All 20 had 1.56- to 10.35-fold stronger contact than a power-law with distance predicts. Pre-trained models are provided for eight input combinations.

items.q: What hinted at enhancer-enhancer interactions in the model?
items.a: The feature for summed activity of other elements within 5 kb of the perturbed element mattered. Removing it significantly lowered performance: precision at 70% recall dropped by 0.01 (P bootstrap = 0.04).
items.info: This conflicts with the ABC model's assumption that enhancers act additively and independently.

items.q: What do they mean by super-additive enhancers?
items.a: Two enhancers that together have a larger effect on gene expression than the sum of their individual effects, in linear expression space. In perturbation experiments this looks 'sub-subtractive': inhibiting both gives a smaller decrease than an additive model expects.

items.q: What evidence for super-additivity came from CRISPRi tiling screens?
items.a: In 20 CRISPRi tiling experiments that perturbed all candidate enhancers near a gene, 10 genes had summed individual enhancer effects above 100%. So at least some enhancer pairs at these loci must act super-additively.
items.info: Only enhancers with significant negative effects (adjusted P < 0.05) that did not overlap promoters were kept. Exception: two PVT1 promoter regions known to act as MYC enhancers.

items.q: What did the pairwise MYC enhancer screen show?
items.a: All pairwise combinations of seven MYC enhancers (e1 to e7) were perturbed in K562 with CRISPRi-FlowFISH. 19 of 21 pairs showed significant super-additive interactions (BH-corrected P < 0.05). Close pairs (3 to 89 kb) with higher Hi-C contact differed from the additive model by 16 to 37%, and distant pairs (107 kb to 1.79 Mb) by only 2 to 10%.
items.info: The authors and others showed that these effects do not appear to be an artefact of CRISPRi spreading (Supplementary Note 1).
items.concl: Nearby enhancers act super-additively, whereas distant enhancers combine roughly additively.

items.q: What orthogonal evidence came from H3K27ac data?
items.a: When enhancers were perturbed (CRISPRi, deletions or genetic variants), H3K27ac at other nearby enhancers dropped on average, and the drop shrank with enhancer-enhancer distance.
items.info: For CRISPRi, the 1-10 kb vs more than 100 kb difference had P = 1.79e-9 (Wilcoxon). Data were new CRISPRi-ChIP-seq at the MYC enhancers plus published data (Fuentes LTR CRISPRi, Huang CRISPR deletions, Delaneau chromatin QTLs).
items.concl: Enhancers close together in the genome often influence each other's chromatin state.

items.q: What simple rules for enhancer-gene regulation do the authors propose?
items.a: To a first approximation, the effect of an enhancer is proportional to its activity times its 3D contact with the promoter (the ABC model). Two more factors tune this: promoters of ubiquitously expressed genes respond less to distal enhancers, and nearby enhancers in close 3D proximity boost each other super-additively.
items.info: Contact frequency depends on genomic distance, loop extrusion and the positions of CTCF sites. Promoter responsiveness seems to be encoded in promoter sequence.
items.concl: Four factors (intrinsic enhancer activity, enhancer-promoter 3D contact, promoter class and enhancer-enhancer interactions) explain a substantial fraction of the effects seen in CRISPR data.

items.q: Did they find evidence for redundant enhancers?
items.a: No. Many enhancers had significant individual effects in single-guide data, and the dual-guide data showed no sub-additive effects. Pairwise effects ranged from roughly additive to roughly multiplicative.
items.info: Earlier studies disagreed, maybe partly because cellular or organismal phenotypes can relate non-linearly to quantitative gene expression.

items.q: What are the limitations of CRISPR data as a gold standard?
items.a: There are few positives in few cell types, and element and gene selection is biased. CRISPR cannot tell direct from indirect effects, may pick up non-enhancer effects, may miss elements that induce rather than maintain expression, and can be underpowered for small effects (e.g. under 25%).
items.info: In theory CRISPRi could also act through other mechanisms, such as spreading of the repressive signal. ENCODE-rE2G may inherit these biases.

items.q: What are the limitations of eQTL and GWAS benchmarks, and what is needed next?
items.a: eQTL data lack cell-type resolution, can miss small effects, include non-enhancer mechanisms, and are uncertain about causal variants. GWAS data are uncertain about causal variants, cell types and target genes. Future work needs larger, unbiased CRISPR and eQTL datasets at single-cell-type resolution, plus gene-level disease information.
items.info: To predict quantitative effects, future models must also account for intrinsic promoter strength, which can vary over several orders of magnitude.
items.concl: The same strategy may work for other gene-regulation problems, such as finding TF target genes or mapping variant effects on chromatin.

items.section: Methods - Data processing and candidate elements
items.q: How were DNase-seq data processed and candidate elements defined?
items.a: Single-end BAMs were filtered with samtools view -F 780 -q 30 and were not deduplicated. Paired-end BAMs used -F 1804 -q 30 -f 2 plus Picard MarkDuplicates v1.126. Peaks were called with MACS2 (--shift -75 --extsize 150 --nomodel) on pooled replicates; after removing blacklisted regions, the top 150,000 peaks were resized to 500 bp around summits.
items.info: 500-bp TSS regions were added and overlaps merged. Elements were classed as promoter (within 500 bp of a TSS), genic or intergenic, and all pairs within 5 Mb were candidates. Genome GRCh38; 20,678 promoters (500 bp around the RefSeq TSS); GENCODE v29. Duplicates were not removed from single-end data because they are hard to detect reliably in high-complexity single-end DNase-seq.

items.section: Methods - Data processing and candidate elements
items.q: How were activity and contact features computed?
items.a: DNase-seq and H3K27ac read counts were computed with bedtools coverage and quantile-normalized to a K562 reference. Activity is the geometric mean of DNase and H3K27ac, when H3K27ac is included. Contact came from cell-type-specific Hi-C or a 'Megamap' aggregating 65 ENCODE Hi-C datasets (ENCSR492BKE).
items.info: Hi-C processing: SCALE normalization, power-law interpolation of low-coverage bins, diagonal replacement, doubly stochastic normalization and a pseudocount. CTCF contact domains were found with a two-state HMM (sklearn.hmm, Python 3.8).

items.q: How was the ENCODE-rE2G logistic regression trained and applied?
items.a: The initial 12 features included first- and second-order terms for activity and contact to capture non-linearity. Features were variance-stabilized with log(|x| + 0.01) and fitted with unregularized logistic regression. Evaluation held out each of 23 chromosomes (1 to 22 and X) in turn; for new cell types, a model trained on all 23 chromosomes was used.
items.info: ABC was run in two configurations. DNase-only activity with Megamap contact was used for all 1,458 biosamples (threshold 0.018). DNase + H3K27ac with cell-type-specific Hi-C was used for K562 and GM12878 (threshold 0.027). Thresholds for all models were set at 70% recall.

items.q: How was the combined K562 CRISPR training set built?
items.a: Three datasets were combined: Nasser (mostly CRISPRi-FlowFISH), Gasperini (Perturb-seq) and Schraivogel (TAP-seq). Perturb-seq and TAP-seq were re-analysed with MAST v1.20.0 (BH FDR < 5%). Power came from negative binomial simulations using DESeq2 v1.34.0 parameters and guide variability sigma = 0.13, with 20 replicates.
items.info: Pairs were kept at 1 kb to 1 Mb from the TSS, excluding elements in promoters or target gene bodies. Negatives needed at least 80% power to detect a 15% decrease (25% for Nasser). Duplicates were resolved by preferring significant results, then highest power.

items.q: How was the held-out CRISPR dataset built?
items.a: Eight screens in five cell types: Perturb-seq in K562, DC-TAP-seq in K562 and WTC11, and CRISPRi-FlowFISH in K562, HCT116, GM12878 and Jurkat. Perturb-seq data were re-analysed with SCEPTRE v0.10.0 at 10% FDR, and pairs already in the training data were removed.
items.info: Positives needed more than 5% effect (Perturb-seq/DC-TAP-seq). Positives without H3K27ac (CTCF, H3K27me3 or no-H3K27ac categories) were removed to focus on enhancer-mediated regulation.

items.q: How did they estimate the probability that a CRISPR hit is a direct effect?
items.a: The indirect rate was measured by testing each distal element against 100 random genes on other chromosomes. The direct rate by distance (50-kb bins within 1 Mb, fitted with a power law) was the observed hit rate minus the indirect rate. P direct(d) = r direct(d) / (r direct(d) + r indirect).
items.info: Where the indirect rate could not be measured, the average empirical rate was used. P direct was used to weight precision-recall curves (yardstick v1.2.0).

items.q: How were the CRISPR benchmark statistics computed?
items.a: CRISPR elements were overlapped with predicted elements matched by gene symbol. Scores were aggregated by sum or max, and elements without a prediction got the minimum score. AUPRC and precision/recall at 70% recall were computed with ROCR v1.0-11, with 95% CIs from 10,000 bootstraps (boot v1.3-28.1).
items.info: Pairwise P values came from bootstrapped deltas with CI inversion (boot.pval v0.7.0). No multiple-testing correction unless stated.

items.q: How were the GWAS and eQTL benchmarks set up?
items.a: GWAS: 94 UK Biobank traits fine-mapped with SuSiE in up to 361,194 people of white British ancestry, using BOLT-LMM or SAIGE, with up to 10 causal variants per region and the MHC excluded. eQTL: GTEx v8 eQTLs fine-mapped with SuSiE (PIP > 0.5), restricted to distal noncoding variants and genes above 1 TPM, across 13 tissues.
items.info: Gene-linking used 560 noncoding credible sets near exactly one gene carrying an independent coding variant (PIP at least 0.5), with 197 blood-trait loci as the main benchmark. Enrichment is relative to 1000 Genomes variants. Heritability enrichment was computed with S-LDSC. Fig. 1 says 96 GWAS traits while the text says 94; unclear.

items.q: How was the pairwise MYC CRISPRi-FlowFISH screen done?
items.a: A library of 10,080 paired sgRNA vectors (hU6 and mU6 dual promoters) targeted e1 to e7, the MYC TSS, two adjacent cCREs and a negative control, with 8 sgRNAs per element paired all-by-all. It was transduced into dox-inducible dCas9-KRAB K562 at MOI about 0.1 (55 million cells per replicate, over 500-fold coverage, two biological replicates), then FlowFISH for MYC and RPL13A and sorting into six bins.
items.info: Guides were counted with Bowtie 2. Non-additivity was tested with a two-sided t-test on the interaction term of Effect = E1 + E2 + E1 x E2. The reporting summary mentions TLNRD1, TeloHAEC and quartile bins, which does not match the Methods (MYC, K562, six bins). It looks like leftover text from another study.

items.text: All models miss weak enhancers, enhancers without H3K27ac, very distal elements (e.g. MYC enhancers about 2 Mb away) and housekeeping-gene enhancers. How much of regulatory architecture is still invisible to models trained on CRISPRi in K562?
What is the mechanism that makes enhancers in close 3D proximity act super-additively and change each other's H3K27ac? Distant enhancers combine additively, so is contact frequency itself the driver?

The minimal input is DNase-seq plus a tissue-averaged Hi-C map. Worth going back to: could a similar CRISPR-trained framework work in species without large CRISPR gold standards (e.g. zebrafish or cavefish)? The paper only tests human cell types.
